questiontext.text:
Goal

Write two decorators, then apply each one to a supplied function with an @ line.

How this works in Python

Java gives you annotations. Put one above a method and the compiler writes it into the class file. No code runs because of it.

@Deprecated
String greet(String name) {
    return "hi " + name;
}

That line is metadata and nothing else. Plain Java SE never acts on it. Some other program has to read the annotation back by reflection, or a framework has to do that reading for you. Without such a tool the annotation changes nothing about what happens when somebody calls greet.

So when you want every reply shouted back at you, you write the wrapping by hand.

String shout(Supplier<String> body) {
    return body.get().toUpperCase();
}

shout(() -> greet("ada"));

Every caller has to remember that. Forget once and one code path answers quietly while the rest shout.

Python attaches the wrapping to the definition instead, and does it once. A decorator is an ordinary function that takes a function and returns a function. There is nothing more exotic to it.

from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Any


def shout(func: Callable[..., Any]) -> Callable[..., Any]:
    def wrapper(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
        return func(*args, **kwargs).upper()
    return wrapper

A function is a value, which is the closures topic, so func is an ordinary parameter holding one. Its annotation is Callable[..., Any], where the dots stand for whatever parameters that function takes. Callable comes from collections.abc and Any comes from typing.

Now apply it. A line starting with @ above a def is what applies a decorator.

@shout
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"hi {name}"

Those four lines mean exactly this, and typing the second spelling yourself gives you the same result.

def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"hi {name}"


greet = shout(greet)

Read the order carefully. Python runs the def statement first and builds the function object. Python then calls shout with that object and rebinds the name greet to whatever comes back. The @ line is shorthand for that one assignment and for nothing else. No reflection reads it, no framework is involved, and nothing rewrites your call sites while the program runs.

The inner wrapper reaches func because it is a closure over the enclosing call, which is the closures topic again. It takes *args and **kwargs, which is the signatures and defaults topic. *args collects any positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs collects any keyword arguments into a dict. Passing both straight through means one wrapper fits any signature you put underneath it, whether that function takes nothing, takes three arguments, or takes keyword-only ones.

The rebinding costs you something. The name greet points at wrapper now, so greet.__name__ reads wrapper. The docstring, which is the string literal on the first line of a function body, has gone with it, so greet.__doc__ is None. A stack trace names wrapper instead of the function that failed. functools.wraps repairs all of that damage, and repairing it is the next tier's lesson. Leave it alone here and meet the damage first.

Your task

Three things sit in the answer box already. CALLS is a module-level list the tests read, and it keeps everything appended to it for the whole run. greet and add are supplied. Write the two decorators, put one @ line above each supplied function, and change nothing inside either body.

  • shout(func) returns a wrapper that calls func and hands back the result with .upper() applied to it.
  • trace(func) returns a wrapper that appends func.__name__ to CALLS, then calls func and hands back its result unchanged.
  • @shout goes above greet and @trace goes above add.

Name both inner functions wrapper, because the tests print that name back at you.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Write each decorator as two def statements, an outer one and an inner one. No class, no lambda.
  • Give the inner wrapper *args and **kwargs and pass both straight through. A wrapper that spells out name fits one function and no other.
  • Apply both decorators with an @ line. The assignment spelling does the same job, and the second test proves it, so read that test before you decide the @ was magic.
  • Leave functools.wraps to the next tier. Meet the lost name and the lost docstring first.
  • Annotate every signature, the wrappers included. A parameter holding a function is Callable[..., Any].
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write two decorator factories, then stack both of them on the supplied read_sensor.

How this works in Python

Java gives you annotations. An annotation does nothing on its own. It records metadata against a declaration, and no code runs because of it.

@Retryable(attempts = 3)
String readSensor(String name) { ... }

Plain Java SE never acts on that line. Some other program has to read the annotation by reflection and rebuild the call. Without such a tool you write the wrapper by hand.

String withRetry(int times, Supplier<String> body) {
    RuntimeException last = null;
    for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) {
        try { return body.get(); }
        catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; }
    }
    throw last;
}

Every caller now has to remember to wrap. Forget once and the retry is gone from that path.

Python attaches the wrapper to the definition instead, once. A decorator is a line starting with @ above a def. The previous tier had you write one that took no arguments of its own. Here yours take arguments. A decorator is an ordinary function that takes a function and returns a function. The type of a function is Callable[..., Any], where the dots stand for whatever parameters it takes, and Callable comes from collections.abc while Any comes from typing.

def shout(func: Callable[..., str]) -> Callable[..., str]:
    def wrapper(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> str:
        return func(*args, **kwargs).upper()
    return wrapper


@shout
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"hi {name}"

The @ line is shorthand and nothing more. Python runs the def greet statement first. Python then runs greet = shout(greet). Type that assignment yourself and you get the same result. No reflection reads the line, and nothing rewrites your call sites while the program runs.

Two features from earlier modules make the wrapper work. The inner wrapper reaches func because it is a closure over the enclosing call, which is the closures topic. It then accepts *args and **kwargs, which is the signatures and defaults topic. *args collects any positional arguments into a tuple, and **kwargs collects any keyword arguments into a dict. Passing both straight through means one wrapper fits any signature.

That rebinding costs you something. The name greet now points at wrapper, so greet.__name__ reads wrapper. The docstring, which is the string literal on the first line of a function body, is gone. A stack trace names wrapper instead of the function that failed.

functools.wraps repairs the damage. Put @functools.wraps(func) on the inner function. It copies __name__, __doc__ and the other identifying attributes across from the original. It also sets __wrapped__ on the wrapper, pointing back at the function underneath.

A decorator that takes an argument needs one more level. @retry(3) calls retry(3) first, and whatever that call returns is used as the decorator. So retry is a function returning a function returning a function. Three def statements, each inside the last.

@audit("ops")
@retry(3)
def read_sensor(name: str) -> str:
    ...

Read a stack of decorators from the bottom up. retry(3) wraps read_sensor first. audit("ops") then wraps that wrapper. So audit sees one call while retry sees every call it makes.

Your task

Five things already sit in the answer box. LOG, ATTEMPTS and PENDING_FAILURES are module-level names the tests read. SensorError is the exception class. read_sensor raises SensorError the first PENDING_FAILURES times you call it. Add two decorator lines above def read_sensor and change nothing inside any of the five.

Write the two decorator factories, then stack them on read_sensor with @audit("ops") above @retry(3). A decorator factory is the outer function, the one you call to get a decorator back. The !r conversion in the log line below is from the strings and f-strings topic. It prints the repr, so a returned string keeps its quotes.

  • audit(channel) appends f"{channel}: calling {func.__name__}" to LOG before the call. When the call returns, it appends f"{channel}: {func.__name__} returned {result!r}" and returns the result. When the call raises, it logs nothing more and lets the exception through.
  • retry(times) calls the function and returns its result. After a SensorError it calls again, up to times calls in total. When every call fails, it raises the last SensorError.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Put @functools.wraps(func) on every wrapper you write. An anonymous wrapper in a stack trace is a defect, and the hidden check fails if __name__ or the docstring changes.
  • Write retry as three nested def statements. No class with __call__, no functools.partial, no shortcut.
  • Add two lines above def read_sensor and change nothing else. The body is not yours to touch.
  • Let the last SensorError out. A retry that swallows the final failure reports a healthy sensor that is not there.
  • Do not write read_sensor = audit("ops")(read_sensor) in your answer. Use the @ lines and let the test prove the two spellings are the same.
  • Annotate every signature, the wrappers included. Three nested def statements with no types on them is a puzzle, not a decorator.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write a forwarding wrapper class, a Protocol with two clock classes, and a log that takes its clock as an argument.

How this works in Python

The Gang of Four Decorator pattern in Java wraps an object instead of a function. You extend the base class so callers still accept you, hold the wrapped instance, and forward every method.

class CountingReader extends Reader {
    private final Reader inner;
    private int reads = 0;

    CountingReader(Reader inner) { this.inner = inner; }

    public int read(char[] buf, int off, int len) throws IOException {
        reads++;
        return inner.read(buf, off, len);
    }

    public void close() throws IOException { inner.close(); }
}

That is one forwarding method per method on the base class. Miss one and the compiler stops you.

Python forwards everything through a single hook. __getattr__ is a dunder method, so Python calls it for you and you never call it by name. Python calls it only after normal attribute lookup has already failed. Write it once, and every name you did not define yourself lands there.

class Recorder:
    def __init__(self, target: object) -> None:
        self.target = target
        self.seen: list[str] = []

    def __getattr__(self, name: str) -> Any:
        self.seen.append(name)
        return getattr(self.target, name)

The built-in getattr(obj, "size") does the same job as obj.size. You supply the name at run time as a string. No base class, no method list, no compiler complaint.

That covers ordinary names. It does not cover len(w), w[0] or a for loop over the wrapper. Python looks those three up on the type and skips the instance entirely. So the lookup never reaches __getattr__. Meet that failure before you fix it. Wrap a list, call len() on the wrapper and read the TypeError. Then define __len__, __getitem__ and __iter__ and nothing else. __iter__ hands back an iterator, so its return type is Iterator[Any] from collections.abc.

Forwarding costs you the type check. isinstance(w, list) answers False, and no amount of forwarding changes that. Java's inheritance buys you the check for free. Python's forwarding does not.

Give a class a __call__ method and its instances become callable. Writing w(4) then runs __call__. That makes the same class usable as an @ line. @Recorder above def scale runs scale = Recorder(scale). The name scale now points at an instance, and calling it lands in __call__.

Now the second half. A Java interface is nominal. A class satisfies Clock only when it writes implements Clock. A third-party class with a matching now() still needs an adapter.

interface Clock { String now(); }

typing.Protocol is structural. A Protocol is a class you inherit from to declare a shape. Any class with a matching now satisfies that shape. The matching class never imports the Protocol and never names it.

from typing import Protocol


class Clock(Protocol):
    def now(self) -> str:
        ...

The ... is the Ellipsis literal from the inheritance and protocols topic, and it is the conventional empty body for a Protocol method. Add @runtime_checkable above the class and isinstance starts working against it. That check tests for the presence of the names and nothing else. A class whose now is a string passes the check and then fails when you call it.

Nothing wires the clock in for you. The constructor parameter is the wiring, and AuditLog(FrozenClock()) is the whole of it. Call datetime.now() inside AuditLog instead and you have a dependency no test can pin down.

Your task

The answer box already holds LOG, the audit decorator from the previous tier, the opening of Recorder down to its __init__, and a supplied scale function. Leave audit alone and leave the body of scale alone. Write the rest.

  • Recorder wraps any object. Every ordinary attribute reached through it appends that name to self.seen and then forwards. __len__, __getitem__ and __iter__ append their own dunder names before forwarding. __call__ appends "__call__" and calls the target.
  • Put @Recorder above @audit("ops") on scale.
  • Clock is a runtime-checkable Protocol with one method, now.
  • SystemClock.now() returns the real time as a string. FrozenClock(stamp) returns the stamp it was built with, and its default stamp is "2026-01-01T09:00:00".
  • AuditLog(clock) stores the clock and an empty entries list. record(message) appends f"{self.clock.now()} {message}" to entries and returns it.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Forward with one __getattr__. Do not subclass the wrapped type, and do not write a method named after one of its methods.
  • Meet the failure before you fix it. Call len() on a wrapper first, read the TypeError, then define exactly the three dunders you need.
  • Leave isinstance(w, list) at False. Write one comment in Recorder saying what that costs you.
  • Neither clock may inherit from anything, and neither may name Clock anywhere in its body.
  • Take the clock through AuditLog's constructor. A datetime call inside AuditLog is a dependency no test can pin down.
  • Annotate every signature you write. self is the one name that never gets one.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.
